questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Function Given in Implicit Form Using the Product Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x) \\ [(x)(\frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{dy}}{\text{d}x})+(1)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(y))] & =2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{y}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2 \\ \frac{x}{y}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y(2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y))}{x}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining an Intercept of a Tangent or Normal Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form
questions.problem: The equation of a curve is $2{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}=8.$ The tangent line at the point $(1,\,1)$ on the curve intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,\,1).$  

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 4x+12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-4x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4x}{12y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & ={(-\frac{x}{3y})}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\cdot 1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-1) & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}(0-1)+1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}+1 \\ y & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,\frac{4}{3}).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Function Given in Implicit Form Using the Product Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x{e}^{y}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x{e}^{y} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ [(x)({e}^{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+(1)({e}^{y})] & =2x \\ x\,{e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{y} & =2x\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x{e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{y} & =2x \\ x{e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x-{e}^{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x-{e}^{y}}{x{e}^{y}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}{y}^{3}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-4y & =6x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}-4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x) \\ [3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{3}]-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{3}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6-2x{y}^{3} \\ (3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6-2x{y}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6-2x{y}^{3}}{3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,0)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(0,\,0)} \\  & ={(\frac{6-2x{y}^{3}}{3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4})}_{(0,\,0)} \\  & =\frac{6-2\cdot 0\cdot {0}^{3}}{3\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot {0}^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{6}{(-4)} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining an Intercept of a Tangent or Normal Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13992403/assets/0c89b1d28ce7692f54e0fbf32c1d99b091e24729c837883523d6150450decb17.png)

The equation $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=20x$ represents an ellipse. The tangent line at the point $(4,4)$ on the ellipse intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

The coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(4,4).$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20x) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20x) \\ 8x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =20 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =20-8x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{20-8x}{2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{10-4x}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & ={(\frac{10-4x}{y})|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =\frac{10-4\cdot 4}{4} \\  & =\frac{(-6)}{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(4,4)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{3}{2}(x-4) \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}(x-4)+4 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}x+10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{3}{2}x+10 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot 0+10 \\ y & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,10).$
